formerTitles: U3.LT4 Relearning: Naming Compounds from Formulas
activity.content:
**What you need to be able to do:** I can compare ionic and covalent compounds.

**Think of lunch money vs. a shared pizza.** If your friend hands you a dollar, the dollar moves from them to you: one gives and one takes. That is an **ionic** bond. If you and a friend split a pizza, nobody gives it away; you both eat from it. That is a **covalent** bond.

**What they are made of.** Metal + nonmetal makes an **ionic compound**. Two or more nonmetals make a **covalent compound**. **Metals sit left of the staircase** on the periodic table; nonmetals are to the right. Hydrogen is a nonmetal even though it sits on the left. Transition metals like iron and copper are still metals. A compound with a **polyatomic ion** is **ionic**, even ammonium (NH₄⁺) compounds with no metal.

**What the electrons do.** Ionic: the metal **transfers** electrons to the nonmetal, making positive and negative **ions** that attract. Covalent: the atoms **share** electrons, making **molecules**. Either way, atoms bond to get a full outer level and be stable.

**Properties (your evidence).** Ionic compounds have **high melting points** (generally above 300 °C), form hard **crystals**, and **conduct electricity when dissolved in water**, because they break into free-moving ions. Covalent compounds have **low melting points**, can be solid, liquid or gas, and **do not conduct** when dissolved, because they stay as whole molecules. Color, mass and where a bottle was stored are **irrelevant evidence**.

**How they are named.** Ionic: metal, then nonmetal with -ide, **no prefixes**, and a **Roman numeral** if the metal has more than one charge (iron(III) chloride). Covalent: **prefixes** count the atoms (sulfur dichloride).

**Worked example 1:** Compare CaCl₂ and SCl₂. Calcium is a metal, so CaCl₂ is ionic: calcium transfers electrons, it is a crystal with a high melting point, and its name is calcium chloride. Sulfur is a nonmetal, so SCl₂ is covalent: the atoms share electrons, it has a low melting point, and its name is sulfur dichloride.

**Worked example 2:** Classify (NH₄)₃PO₄ (ammonium is NH₄⁺, phosphate is PO₄³⁻). Every atom is a nonmetal, but it is made of polyatomic ions, so it is **ionic**.

**Worked example 3:** An unknown melts at 80 °C and its solution does not light the bulb. 80 °C is far below 300 °C, and no conductivity means no free ions. Both point to **covalent**.

**Watch out for:** calling an ammonium compound covalent just because it has no metal, calling hydrogen a metal, calling two metals ionic, forgetting that transition metals are metals, putting prefixes on an ionic name, and using color, mass or "it dissolves" as evidence. Use melting point and conductivity instead.
prompts: Compare NaCl and CO₂. For each one, say what kind of elements it is made of and what the electrons do.
A student says, "This unknown is ionic because it is white and dissolves in water." Explain what is wrong with the evidence and name two tests that would actually decide.
MgCl₂ is named magnesium chloride, but SCl₂ is named sulfur dichloride. Explain why the two names follow different rules.
Salt water lights the bulb on a conductivity tester, but sugar water does not. Explain why.
